A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoTrust. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching detailed evaluations moved into v2's appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of six VLMs across trustfulness, safety, robustness, privacy, and fairness, with detailed numerical results in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical evaluations and adds human validation, additional robustness results, and backbone and fine-tuning experiments.

M1.justification: The core benchmark framework and evaluated models' procedures are retained. Algorithm 1 documents the previously described replacement of coordinate references with object descriptions; it does not establish a changed method. The new fine-tuned LLaVA variant is an experimental case study.

E1.justification: The eight driving datasets, Single-DriveLM, and tested languages are retained. v2 adds compression, contrast, and pixelation scenarios to visual robustness evaluation and uses MME perception and cognition tasks in Appendix J, modestly extending coverage beyond the original driving evaluations.

E2.justification: The six principal evaluated models remain unchanged. Appendix J adds a direct comparison between LLaVA-v1.6 and LLaMA-Adapter V2.1 on MME, plus comparisons with a supervised-fine-tuned LLaVA variant. These comparisons were absent from v1.

E3.justification: v2 introduces two human evaluation protocols: three annotators inspect 10% samples from five datasets, and three annotators rate 100 LLaVA answers. It also adds BIM/C&W attack settings, severity-3 image corruptions, and one-epoch LoRA fine-tuning on 1,000 NuScenes-QA samples. The main white-box summary now averages three attacks instead of reporting PGD alone.

E4.justification: New analyses test generated-question quality, agreement between GPT and human scoring, robustness beyond PGD and Gaussian noise, and possible explanations for generalist superiority. Appendix E also diagnoses EM-VLM4AD's repeated-option responses, while Appendix J examines backbone differences and specialization through fine-tuning. These substantially extend v1's supporting analyses.

E5.justification: Section 9 introduces statistical validation through a human–GPT agreement estimate, reporting PLCC from answers independently rated by three annotators. v1 contains no corresponding agreement analysis. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-model-run variability.

E6.justification: Most original numerical results survive unchanged in the appendices. Substantial additions include QA acceptance rates of 84.62–90.74% in Table 8, human–GPT PLCC of 0.8726, BIM/C&W results, three additional corruption conditions, and MME/fine-tuning results in Tables 35–37. These are new results, not established same-setting improvements over v1; Table 37's DriveLM baseline conflicts with Table 11.

T1.justification: The substantive scoring, uncertainty, fairness, and PGD mathematics remain unchanged. The new Gaussian-noise equation restates the existing procedure, and adding the ground-truth argument to the PGD loss is not a substantive mathematical revision. Neither version presents theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The benchmark contribution, five-dimensional scope, and overall generalist-superiority claim remain. The highlighted safety claim changes: v1 associates greater vulnerability with smaller models, whereas v2 emphasizes universal vulnerability and larger models' susceptibility to contextual attacks through instruction following.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies v1's interpretation of EM-VLM4AD's strong adversarial resistance by attributing it to collapsed predictions. Section 9 and Appendix J expand explanations of generalist superiority through alignment, backbone capabilities, and specialization effects. New qualifications address GPT evaluation and limited generalist coverage, although some older, conflicting interpretations remain in the appendices.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds substantial construction details: sampling rules, distractor generation, YOLOv10n coordinate mapping, CoVLA downsampling, question-type proportions, and frame-relevance prompts. New experiments disclose LoRA parameters, attack budgets, and corruption software/settings. These are chiefly added documentation; existing hardware and training descriptions are relocated. v2 omits v1's exact GPT scoring prompt and explicit leaderboard link.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes AutoTrust from DriveBench and SCD-Bench, adds literature supporting GPT-based evaluation, and updates coverage of collaborative driving and other recent VLM research. The central positioning as a comprehensive driving-trustworthiness benchmark, including its relationship to CARES, remains.

P1.justification: The main narrative is extensively condensed and rewritten into short setup/result summaries. Detailed evaluations, model descriptions, metrics, related work, limitations, and social impacts are reorganized into appendices. A dedicated discussion section and separate conclusion replace v1's combined closing structure, and the contents page is removed.

P2.justification: v2 introduces consolidated main-text tables, an aggregate fairness scatter plot, and a vehicle-fairness heat map. Existing charts move to appendices, paired fairness radar charts become separate figures, and privacy tables split by shot count. New validation, attack, and fine-tuning tables accompany a document-wide journal-layout change.

improvement.justification: Human checks of question quality and GPT scoring address validation gaps in v1, while expanded construction details and the response-collapse analysis improve reproducibility and interpretation. Reporting problems limit these gains: Appendix E describes additional attacks on NuScenes-QA while Section 4 presents an across-dataset summary, and Table 37 reports a DriveLM baseline of 66.78 versus 73.59 in Table 11. The net improvement is useful but limited by unresolved inconsistencies.
